Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}
contenu:
Format : long
Limite de longueur : 4500 caractères au total.
Édition numérique, lue sur téléphone, sans contrainte de page : la limite suit la matière disponible dans la source. Adapte le nombre de sections à la longueur : 2 sections sous 2 000 caractères, 3 ou 4 jusqu'à 3 500, 4 à 6 au-delà ; même règle de longueur (90 à 100 % de la limite). N'étire jamais une source mince : mieux vaut un article court et exact.
Travail de recherche : utilise EXACTEMENT ces intertitres, dans cet ordre : « La question » (pourquoi ce travail, d'après l'introduction) ; « Les conclusions » (principaux résultats, avec les chiffres) ; « La méthode » (données et démarche, en quelques phrases) ; « Ce que ça implique » (explication accessible des conséquences, telles que les auteurs les présentent) ; « Les limites » (uniquement celles mentionnées par les auteurs ; omets cette section s'ils n'en mentionnent aucune). Remplis « reference » : auteurs, institution ou revue, date, et nature du document (document de travail non relu par des pairs, article de revue à comité de lecture, billet de chercheur…), uniquement d'après le texte fourni.
Source : PLOS Climate
Rubrique : Climat
Date du flux : 23/11/2026
Auteur : Maggie Jones; Anu Ramachandran; Annie B Rosenthal; Mira Miles; Donya Zarrinnegar; Jen Monroe Zakaras; Noam Shimon; Arianne Teherani; Sheri D Weiser
Titre d'origine : Extreme heat and wildfire smoke: Operational vulnerabilities and workforce strain in California healthcare facilities

ARTICLE :
Figures
Abstract
Background
Extreme heat and wildfire smoke events are increasing in frequency, severity, and geographic reach, placing compounding strain on healthcare systems and workers. Despite growing recognition of these events as public health threats, critical gaps persist in our understanding of how frontline healthcare providers perceive facility preparedness and operational impacts, their access to resources, and their experiences of these events.
Objective
To explore frontline healthcare provider knowledge of emergency preparedness plans and resource availability for extreme heat and wildfire smoke events, and to characterize their perceptions of how these events affect patients, staff, and clinical operations at healthcare facilities in the San Francisco Bay Area.
Methods
Semi-structured interviews with 29 healthcare providers were conducted between June 2023 and December 2024. Interviews were conducted remotely over Zoom, recorded, and transcribed verbatim. Analysis followed a hybrid inductive-deductive approach using Dedoose qualitative research software, with each transcript double coded by two investigators.
Results
Four themes emerged. First, infrastructural inadequacies, including insufficient cooling and ventilation, equipment failures, and unreliable backup power, create cascading impacts on patient safety, staff comfort, and operational efficiency that disproportionately affect emergency departments, urgent care settings, and community clinics. Second, healthcare workers, especially outdoor and safety-net clinic workers, experience significant physical, psychological, logistical, and caregiving burdens during these events. Third, health systems, many of which are already operating at or near capacity, experience substantial operational strain, driven by increased emergency department volumes and acuity, delayed discharges, and heightened cognitive demands on staff. Fourth, knowledge of facility emergency plans was limited and siloed among most respondents, with resource management frequently described as improvised and unsupported by clear institutional guidance.
Conclusions
Extreme heat and wildfire smoke events create compounding, systems-level threats to the functioning of Bay Area healthcare facilities that are inadequately addressed by current preparedness frameworks. Findings point to the need for climate-ready infrastructure, anticipatory staffing models, structured communication between leadership and frontline staff, and institutional recognition of the importance of preparing for these events.
Citation: Jones M, Ramachandran A, Rosenthal AB, Miles M, Zarrinnegar D, Zakaras JM, et al. (2026) Extreme heat and wildfire smoke: Operational vulnerabilities and workforce strain in California healthcare facilities. PLOS Clim 5(11): e0001098. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pclm.0001098

Introduction
Climate-sensitive disasters, such as wildfires and heatwaves, are increasing in frequency, duration, severity, and geographic distribution. The number of heatwave days in the US has tripled since 1960, and severe wildfires are projected to increase by 30% globally by 2050 [1,2]. These exposures often co-occur, creating compounded hazards that synergistically and disproportionately harm the health of vulnerable populations [3]. Health impacts include short-term increases in both emergency department utilization and in hospitalizations, as well as longer-term sequelae such as worsened cardiopulmonary health, disruptions in care, and mental health challenges, all of which are made worse by repeated exposures [4–8].
California’s environmental landscape presents unprecedented challenges for public health, with rising temperatures and prolonged drought conditions creating conditions for increasingly frequent and severe extreme heat events and wildfires [9,10]. Wildfires have become the leading source of ambient fine particulate matter (PM2.5) across the state, with recent events resulting in billions of dollars in damages and exposing millions of residents to hazardous air quality [10,11]. The increasing frequency and long-tail effects of extreme heat and wildfire smoke are putting significant new strains on healthcare systems and workers, which must adapt to these circumstances in order to effectively provide care during and following these events. Most disaster planning focuses on single events and related patient “surges” [12–14], but climate-related events are increasingly common, often recur seasonally, and frequently overlap, challenging conventional paradigms of disaster management [15,16]. These events also compromise the safety and functionality of health facility infrastructure, as well as the psychological and physical capacity of the healthcare workforce that is often subject to the same strains as patients.
Despite growing recognition of extreme heat and wildfire smoke as public health threats, critical knowledge gaps persist regarding how these events affect health system infrastructure and operations, whether and how facility-level preparedness strategies are implemented, and what barriers frontline healthcare workers face in providing climate-informed care [17,18]. Importantly, there is limited qualitative research capturing the perspectives of healthcare providers during extreme heat and wildfire smoke events, and this data is crucial to addressing operational and training needs, resource allocation, practical workflows, and implementation efforts critical to successful response on the ground.
This study addresses these knowledge gaps by exploring what frontline healthcare workers can tell us about current state of clinical and operational preparedness of healthcare facilities in the San Francisco Bay Area for extreme heat and wildfire smoke events. Through in-depth interviews with frontline healthcare workers in these Bay Area facilities, we aim to characterize existing heat and smoke preparedness plans, understand provider knowledge and training needs, identify resource needs and implementation barriers, and document provider experiences providing care during these climate hazards. Capturing a rich and diverse range of perspectives provides essential insights into the practical, real-world challenges of implementing preparedness strategies at the facility level—information that is largely absent from the current literature but critical for developing effective, context-specific adaptation measures.
Methods
Ethics statement
This study was approved by the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) Institutional Review Board (IRB 22–38277), including approval of the use of verbal informed consent. Participants were given a study information sheet prior to the interview that described the purpose of the study and what participation would entail. If they expressed interest in participating, a Zoom video interview was scheduled. At the beginning of each interview, the interviewer reviewed information about the study and answered any participant questions. Participants then provided voluntary informed verbal consent, which was documented by the interviewer in the study records.
Study design and setting
From June 2023 to December 2024, we conducted a qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with healthcare providers in the San Francisco Bay Area. This region represents a critical setting for examining healthcare facility preparedness for climate-related events. The region has experienced multiple significant wildfires, including the 2017 North Bay fires and the 2018 Camp Fire, which exposed millions of residents to hazardous air quality and resulted in substantial increases in respiratory hospitalizations [19–21]. In terms of temperatures, the region’s historically temperate coastal climate has made its infrastructure and populations inadequately adapted to extreme heat. Notably, the region’s healthcare facilities serve diverse populations with varying vulnerabilities to heat and smoke exposures, including communities with limited resources for individual-level protective measures.
The Bay Area includes nine counties served by a diverse array of health systems, from quaternary academic medical centers to safety-net hospitals run by departments of public health and private community hospitals. All face recurrent and overlapping climate-related extreme weather events, including extreme heat exacerbated by limited cooling infrastructure, wildfire smoke from regional and distant fires that PM2.5 levels, and atmospheric rivers that produce extreme precipitation and flooding that disrupts infrastructure.
Participants and recruitment
Eligible participants were healthcare providers who interfaced with patients in clinical or nonclinical roles at facilities in the San Francisco Bay Area. Participants were classified as “internal” (UCSF providers across campus locations) or “external” (community-based providers from San Francisco Department of Public Health [SFDPH] community clinics and other nonprofit care settings in any of the nine Bay Area counties). We aimed to recruit approximately equal numbers of participants from hospital and community health settings; however, despite substantial outreach efforts, fewer community-based providers overall were enrolled.
We used purposive sampling to capture varied clinical experience, expertise, and institutional roles within the healthcare settings. We were particularly interested in recruiting participants who held leadership or administrative positions in addition to their clinical roles, given their potential insights into the development and deployment of facility emergency response plans, as well as participants involved in climate-specific planning efforts (e.g., clinic-based working groups).
The study team compiled an initial list of potential participants based on referrals from project stakeholders, including UCSF faculty and SFDPH partners. Prospective participants were then contacted via email using a standardized recruitment script. Snowball sampling supplemented purposive recruitment; prospective participants were encouraged to share the invitation with interested colleagues, and interviewees asked at the conclusion of each interview to suggest additional contacts. Participants received no compensation.
Data collection
A semi-structured interview guide was developed by a team of three investigators (MM, JMZ, SDW) based on the study aims, a review of the literature, and insights from internal and external stakeholders [22–24]. Questions addressed providers’ experiences delivering care during extreme heat and wildfire smoke events, whether their facility had an emergency plan for these event types, and what resources were available or would be helpful for mitigating impacts. Interviewees were also invited to share anecdotes about experiences with other types of weather events. Interviews also covered barriers and facilitators to implementation of recommended public health strategies for preventing adverse health effects from climate-related events [25].
One-on-one interviews were conducted in English remotely using Zoom video. One of three investigators (ABR, NS, MM) conducted each interview, and all were trained by investigators (SDW, JMZ) on conducting qualitative in-depth interviews, covering skills such as rapport building, probing for details, and reflecting clarity of participants’ ideas. None of the investigators were known by the participants prior to data collection. Interviews lasted between 11 and 43 minutes. Interviews were recorded and transcribed verbatim, and field notes were generated from each session. Data were de-identified following analysis and all participants were assigned unique identification numbers.
Analysis
We used an inductive-deductive thematic approach to analyze the transcribed interviews [26].. This hybrid approach is especially well-suited to exploring relatively novel topics where some theoretical grounding exists, but the specific context remains underexplored. In this case, we sought to systematically characterize existing extreme heat and wildfire smoke preparedness plans and identify anticipated resource needs within established disaster management frameworks, while also enabling inductive exploration of emergent themes from frontline healthcare workers’ perspectives and experiences that may not be captured by existing frameworks and may reveal unanticipated barriers, facilitators, and experiential insights.
An initial codebook was developed by (MM, JMZ, NS) under the guidance of (SDW), based on the study aims and questions explored in the interview guide. The codebook was pilot-tested by (MM, JMZ, NS), each of whom coded a subset of transcripts and then met to compare coding, discuss discrepancies, and refine code definitions.
The broader analytic team (JMZ, MJ, ABR, MM, SDW) iteratively revised the codebook by reviewing transcripts and adding new inductive codes to capture emergent themes not reflected in the original deductive framework. They met regularly to review emergent codes, discuss their application, and reach consensus on the final codebook.
All transcripts were coded using Dedoose software (Los Angeles, CA: SocioCultural Research Consultants, LLC www.dedoose.com). Each transcript was double coded by two investigators (JMZ, DZ), and code application was iteratively reviewed and discussed until consensus was achieved to maximize coding reliability. Discrepancies between coders were discussed and iteratively reviewed until consensus was reached. Coded excerpts were then aggregated by code, and patterns across codes were organized into themes and subthemes through team discussion and review. Selected participant quotations were chosen to illustrate key findings.
Results
Twenty-nine participants were enrolled in the study. Twenty-four (82.8%) were physicians, three (10.3%) were nurses, one (3.4%) was a paramedic, and one (3.4%) was a community health worker. The majority (19, 65.5%) were hospital-based providers, eight (27.6%) worked in community clinics, and two (6.9%) held joint positions. Among physicians, the most common specialties included internal medicine (N = 5), pediatrics (N = 5), emergency medicine (N = 4), and family medicine (N = 3).
Infrastructure as vulnerability
According to informants, historically temperate weather in the Bay Area has led to lack of air conditioning in most homes and public facilities, increasing the area’s vulnerability to the health effects of extreme heat and poor air quality. This inadequacy in community infrastructure was felt to increase both patient and staff vulnerability as well as to increase pressure on health systems at relatively lower temperatures. Providers described infrastructural vulnerability in terms of community infrastructure and lower heat thresholds, Inadequate facility Infrastructure causing exposure, impacts on equipment, power outages, and the benefits of updated infrastructure.
Community infrastructure and lower heat thresholds. Informants described differences in regional infrastructure that can shift the temperature at which health impacts begin to emerge, with lower temperatures leading to heat-related impacts in the Bay Area. As stated by one provider:
I’m originally from the East Coast where every summer, it would be mayhem when the temperatures would get above 90 or so…in the Bay Area, we have a much lower threshold, because…so much of the population does not have access to air conditioning at home. (Physician, Hospital)
Inadequate facility Infrastructure causing exposure: Infrastructural inadequacies within healthcare facilities themselves, both large- and small-scale, were frequently described to limit the facility’s response during heat and wildfire smoke events and facilitate exposures to heat and poor air quality in clinical settings. Even when air conditioning was available, heat and poor air quality could overwhelm current cooling and HVAC equipment. Multiple respondents described how these exposures negatively affect patient safety and patient experience and have impacts on provider and staff comfort while performing daily tasks both in clinical and non-clinical areas (Table 1).
Emergency rooms and hospital lobbies were particularly vulnerable to poor air quality due to frequent intrusions of outside air from in-and-out traffic, as described by one physician.
We run HVAC systems, but the doors open widely [and] frequently to let in ambulance traffic. And we definitely have a problem with poor quality air intruding into the emergency department forcing providers to wear N95s...It is difficult to keep the temperatures cool, in normal working temperature, when it’s very hot outdoors, and it’s particularly difficult in the emergency department where you can’t keep the doors closed, because of ambulance traffic and patients coming and going. (Physician, Hospital)
Participants noted that settings serving higher-risk patient populations with inadequate infrastructural support, such as skilled nursing facilities or carceral institutions, may be particularly impacted (Table 1). As one provider described,
I think there are times where it feels like the [skilled nursing] facility’s ability to handle extreme heat seems limited... I’m very worried that ...if we had extreme heat, I don’t think our air conditioning...is equipped enough to meet appropriate cooling needs…The majority of the patients are generally older adults. And so they are more predisposed to extreme heat events...they’re at the rehab because they’re recovering after the hospital, they’re not fully healthy and at home. So they’re a vulnerable group in terms of heat related illnesses. (Physician, Hospital and Community Clinic)
Impacts on equipment. Other impacts within facilities included forced closure of uncooled inpatient units and failure of laboratory equipment, which resulted in outsourcing of lab tests and subsequent care delays and costs. Impacts extended to faulty ice machines, impacting the ability to keep patients comfortable on uncooled hospital floors. Providers also described direct impacts on clinical care when equipment requiring stable temperatures was compromised (Table 1). As one provider described,
We can’t give any vaccines because opening the fridge would then decrease the temperature below which or above which we can keep vaccines safely.... if the fridge temperature were to increase, then we would have to dump the thousands, tens of thousands of dollars worth of vaccines. (Physician, Community Clinic)
Power outages. There were also concerns about inadequate preparation for power outages. Not all facilities had adequate back-up power strategies, though some reported active work to mitigate this at their facilities. Multiple providers noted how power outages during extreme weather events significantly impact the ability to provide care (Table 1). As one provider described,
During the excessive rains this year, which I think are likely linked to climate change we had a power outage. When the power goes out in the hospital, only electrical outlets that are colored red continue to function.. Unfortunately, what we learned was that our clinic and urgent care, which sees relatively high acuity patients, did not have any red plugs. And it definitely raised some concern that we weren’t ready for this kind of eventuality. (Physician, Hospital)
Benefits of updated infrastructure. While most interviewees cited specific infrastructural concerns, few felt that achieving the necessary improvements was within their control or that improvements were keeping up with the increasing frequency of these events. Conversely, those who worked in facilities with updated infrastructure consistently noted its positive impact.
Our facility underwent a huge renovation…it’s really become night and day because our ventilation underwent a huge renovation as well. So we have really excellent ventilation and air filtration, heating and cooling. So now I feel like we could be potentially a resource. And that was definitely not the case before we underwent renovation. (Physician, Community Clinic)
Healthcare staff impacts
Impacts on healthcare staff during heat and poor air quality events were multifaceted and included direct effects on staff as members of the community as well as secondary impacts on their ability to perform their health system roles. Staff impacts were often described in terms of conflicting personal and professional responsibilities, physical toll, logistical impacts, impacts on ability to provide effective care, conflict between patient care and staff safety, and emotional strain (Table 2).
Conflicting personal and professional responsibilities. A common theme involved conflicting responsibilities. For example, providers may be caregivers for affected elders and children or need to assume unplanned care during the workday due to school closures, adding a source of significant additional stress.
For me, on a personal level, during the wildfires, I had a newborn at home. So that definitely added stress in terms of I knew that we were in the East Bay, we were nowhere near like the fires into like danger zones. But the air quality concerned me because I was thinking of how can I get the best air quality for my newborn in my house. And so we set up filters and stuff, but I was at work. So... that’s kind of the stressor there. (Nurse, Hospital)
Some respondents also had the impression that this stress may be especially pertinent for lower-resourced clinic staff, who may face greater disparities in access to protective resources at home (Table 2).
Physical toll on staff. Staff also described the direct physical burden of working through extreme heat and poor air quality, including fatigue, irritability, and dehydration (Table 2). As one provider described,
[When] we have a day, 80 something degrees outside, the offices might be 85, 90 degrees or more inside. And so, I find myself and I think a lot of staff, we get tired, we get irritable, we get sweaty, you know, it’s just really uncomfortable. I think the level of stress in the clinic is just generally higher under those circumstances. (Physician, Hospital)
Logistical impacts on staff. Heat and poor air quality events also created logistical barriers that prevented staff from reaching work altogether, from evacuations and road closures to hazardous commuting conditions. When staff were unable to work at their usual sites, providers also described downstream effects on staffing levels and, in some cases, on patient access to care (Table 2).
Impacts on ability to provide effective care. Indoor workers reported being most affected when cooling or air filtration in their facility was inadequate, with significant impacts on their ability to work effectively during heat events. As one provider described,
I do manage a team that do...central lines…their workspace has no AC so…it could be 90 degrees...When they do procedures...they are fully gowned and draped and they get their cap, the masks on, the goggles on, and they basically bake themselves in that attire as well as with PPE. So it’s really difficult when they’re inserting [a] line or [the] position is important. You get sweat dripping down your eyes and you can barely [see] it and you need to hit that [vein]. So it’s definitely a true challenge with the heat. That impacts directly our staff and our patient care and family and satisfaction. (Physician, Hospital)
Conflict between patient care and staff safety. Staff safety and patient care were sometimes in direct conflict, especially, but not only for outdoor workers. Providers reported having to weigh the risks to their staff with the desire to maintain services for their patients, as well as concerns for increased violence towards staff members (Table 2). For example, street medicine teams work outdoors, but might be unsafe doing so during extreme heat or wildfire smoke days when patients most need support.
I think the biggest test...was during the COVID pandemic...there was a pandemic going on, but there was also one of the largest wildfires in California history...we still had to do COVID outreach testing, engaging patients. But when the air quality index was so poor how do we weigh the benefit of sending out a team when the AQI was like above 100 sometimes above 150 right? So, and weighing that with the need to deliver patient care, and then also realizing that our patients that are more vulnerable to extreme heat events and also wildfire smoke, for example, respiratory illnesses, even cardiac illnesses. (Physician, Community Clinic)
Emotional strain. Staff reported being deeply emotionally impacted by the experience of living and working through these climate events (Table 2). They described being distracted by worry about the situation, both in the immediate sense and in terms of its future implications. As one provider described,
The wildfire smoke...it’s orange outside, the air was so filled with smoke that it was hard to breathe, just walking around. That was a major kind of wake-up call, and also [had an] emotional impact to our staff. Because I mean, it was visible, it was so kind of intimidating. It was quite scary. (Paramedic, Hospital)
System overload
Subjects agreed that clinical facilities are critical parts of community disaster response, including the response to climate and extreme weather events and their health impacts. Increased patient volumes, particularly in emergency department and critical care settings, and frequent callouts by staff were reported as drivers of health system strain. Providers described these impacts in terms of increased patient volume and acuity, inconsistent recognition of impact, labor intensive response measures, systemic capacity impacts, ad hoc response and use of available resources, and downstream impact of closures on patient access. (Table 3).
Increased patient volume and acuity. Emergency department providers in particular felt strongly that heat and poor air quality led to significant increases in patient volumes and acuity that was often overwhelming.
We had an event... when there was a heatwave...in San Francisco. And although the ambient temperature was not much above 100 degrees, we had 18 codes in the space of about an hour or an hour and a half from heat stroke, heat exhaustion, people, you know, largely elderly patients, but coming in with seizures, and extreme body temperatures of up to 107 degrees. (Physician, Hospital)
Since the tertiary care university system serves a wide geographic area, patient volumes were also described as being affected by more remote weather events, including influxes of patients seeking relief from poor air quality in other regions (Table 3).
Inconsistent recognition of impacts. In contrast, inpatient clinicians did not consistently report direct impacts of these events on admissions. One interviewed surgeon did not recall any cancellations or delays during extreme heat or poor air quality events. Medical inpatient services generally did not attribute changes in patient census to heat or smoke, though such connections were sometimes recognized retrospectively. Underlying patterns in access to care and delayed clinical effects may shape whether changes in patient volume were attributed to heat and air quality events, as one provider described:
The wildfire smoke. It’s interesting. No, I didn’t see an uptick in asthma exacerbations at that time, during the most recent surge in 2020. However, that was at a time when shelter in place orders were standard. And patients were quite reluctant to come to care. And we were encountering a number of phone calls from patients asking for medication refills. And on further questioning, we realized that many of those children were actively having asthma exacerbations that ordinarily would have come to clinic. So I think that we severely underreported the respiratory impact of wildfire smoke during that wildfire season in 2020. (Physician, Hospital)
Labor intensive response measures. In addition to patient flow impacts on the larger health system, caring for patients during heat and wildfire smoke events adds additional tasks to staff’s daily responsibilities. Among affected staff, cognitive demand was increased, including finding workarounds for infrastructure failures and developing ad hoc means of supporting patient care activities (Table 3). Routine tasks often took longer or caused more discomfort during these events, as one nurse described:
I see that staff not only are trying to coordinate the care that a patient needs, but they’re also trying to address the discomfort that patients are in because it’s too hot, or they’re trying to also not only address it, but also help to mitigate it. So they spend some time cooling, getting equipment to help cool patients down, opening windows, trying to perhaps give baths to help cool patients down. (Nurse, Hospital)
Although fans, ice packs, and cooling blankets were available for inpatient services, infection control policies, intended to improve patient safety under normal circumstances, often posed barriers to implementing heat mitigation strategies such as fans.
For fans…it’s not super helpful, [it’s] warm air...but we’re not allowed to use fans in inpatient rooms, for infection control reasons. Because you circulate germs and bacteria and dust. Or if it’s a private room, you can use it, but you have to close the patient’s door and on a heated day, patients will not want you to close the door for that circulation. So you know we’re losing battles for the hot months in those units. (Nurse, Hospital)
Ad hoc response and use of available resources.
This lack of formal and integrated guidance and planning has led to significant improvisation and innovation with respect to both planning and response. For example, a carceral facility in the region now identifies high-risk patients in a registry ahead of time to minimize health impacts during these events.
During events, providers described providing patients with what resources they had on hand, including physical supplies such as masks or water, as well as information about cooling centers and health and air quality safety. When institutional resources were not available, especially in smaller outpatient clinics, many used their own resources to purchase extra fans, air filters, or air quality monitors.
We quite literally bought air purifiers. Like, my parents donated an air purifier because they had an extra one. We responded in the immediate sense, we were like, we’ve got to get this smoke out and be able to open a clinic. And so... [we] got on Amazon and ordered room air purifiers. (Physician, Hospital)
Several providers also noticed the efforts of facilities and engineering in setting up ad hoc mitigation strategies, like setting up air scrubbers at entrances, though opinions on effectiveness varied. Providers also described improvisational use of equipment for patient care, with one provider describing using body bags to bring in extra ice to lay out on gurneys to cool patients. Organized responses in some facilities and clinics involved similarly high-effort interventions, including individual checks on patients or converting visits to telehealth whenever possible to protect patients.
What we try to do is in the mornings, we try to call everyone in and say, hey, we’re gonna change it to telehealth don’t come in, it’s very dangerous outside. Especially when you have patients that are in chronic care management... you don’t want them to come in and expose themselves. So what we ended up doing, it’s full team effort, we get eligibility workers, health workers like myself, MA’s, we all get a list... let’s get all the morning patients called in. Whether that be, you know, 40 60, 80 patients that we’re calling in that morning, we call them and we let them know don’t come in. (Community Health Worker, Community Clinic)
Systemic capacity Impacts. Clinician concerns about patient safety and risk of readmission may delay discharge and drive prolonged lengths of stay, given a sense that more patients return to the hospital, or “bounce back,” during these events (Table 3). These concerns may prolong patient surge status, increase overcrowding, and further delay access to care. This hesitancy was clearest among clinicians caring for especially vulnerable patients, such as newborns, where discharge may be delayed if conditions in the community feel unsafe. One pediatrician described,
Having to make plans or adjust discharges for babies and their families because of how poor the outdoor air quality is, like asking if the family can leave between this hour and this hour, because it seems like that’s when the smoke is going to clear a little bit. (Physician, Hospital)
Many participants agreed that systems constantly operating at capacity limits flexibility and thus the ability to respond to these emergencies.
We do recognize that every one of these events impacts the emergency department directly, because [it’s] really the only place people have to go when any event occurs. Again, the medical system is at its breaking point, I would say or at least certainly at capacity. And so the idea that we have this added capacity to accommodate the increased visits that inevitably come with heat waves or air pollution issues, is I think naive, I think we have to accept that we are operating at maximum capacity. So when those happen, they do tend to overwhelm us. (Physician, Hospital)
Downstream impact of closures on patient access. There were also significant concerns raised about the downstream impact on patients of shutting down services in response to unsafe conditions.
I will say, though, that there was...the legendary orange day that we had in San Francisco where there was a lot of chatter in our leadership group about whether to even open clinic, reasoning that patients might think this is like the end of days, it was so bizarre. And there were a couple of days when the air quality index was so bad and so severe, that we considered closing for the safety, both of patients and of providers. But the reality of our practice is that closing is not an option. There are too many stakeholders that depend on us being open, especially for urgent care. (Physician, Hospital)
Similar dilemmas arose when facility conditions themselves became unsafe for continued operation, whether due to indoor heat or understaffing, forcing providers to weigh continued operation against safety for both patients and staff (Table 3).
Planning Gaps: Variability and operational uncertainty
Finally, providers described substantial variability in their awareness of, and confidence in, emergency plans for heat and poor air quality events, shaped by limited awareness of emergency plans, lack of guidance around best practices, and lack of prioritization and funding for climate emergencies. Community level response and preparation were also described. (Table 4).
Limited awareness of emergency plans. Most respondents endorsed knowing little to nothing about the specifics of emergency planning for their facility’s operations during heat and AQI events, including whether such plans exist, who develops them, and who to reach out to with questions or issues arising during these events (Table 4).
And I think that was the first time I remember that our division felt the impact of how close it was and that we didn’t have a disaster plan ready...But it’s hard to say, well, we have a disaster plan. But do we ever practice it? Do I know what’s in it? And I’m going to be honest, I don’t know what’s in it. (Physician, Hospital)
Those who felt more confident about emergency preparedness often developed this knowledge in roles outside their clinical scope. Providers working directly in emergency planning or alongside local public health departments were generally aware of current facility and county plans, such as Hospital Incident Command System (HICS) activation, Mass Casualty Incident (MCI) policies, and All-Hazards approaches, and cited a range of outreach channels, including fliers, media alerts, and disaster preparedness websites, though uptake of these resources was variable.
Nevertheless, despite being aware of and sometimes participating in planning, many providers remained concerned that they were inadequately prepared.
So there’s, I would say, pretty extensive planning, and sort of stockpiling of resources, although it’s difficult to always predict both the severity and the length of these climate related surges when they happen. So we do a lot of planning, but it always still feels like we’re still somewhat unprepared when it actually happens. (Physician, Hospital)
Lack of guidance around best practices. Providers felt that city or county planning and community education can mitigate patient surges. However, local clinics often lacked clarity and guidance around best practices, including thresholds for enacting plans or closing clinics. Clinician leaders felt inadequately prepared or supported when managing operations during these events, often feeling that decisions were being made ad hoc and in isolation (Table 4)
Lack of prioritization and funding for climate emergencies. Providers cited several barriers to planning and mitigation, including insufficient information and funding, unclear responsibility for planning, and limited confidence in their ability to undertake it. Conflicting priorities were also seen as a barrier to addressing climate events; some noted that local departments of public health had focused their efforts on COVID-19 response during the pandemic, so that guidance related to disaster preparedness had not been prioritized. Earthquake preparation was also seen as a higher priority (Table 4).
Limited and deprioritized planning and resource allocation in these larger institutions was sometimes attributed to a perception that climate related events are rare or not locally impactful. The unpredictability of the events was seen as a barrier to an effective and organized response; also mentioned were the difficulty of budgeting for equipment that sits in storage, lack of funding or personnel during events, and lack of funding for preparedness efforts in general (Table 4).
